explanations: terra: The God-fearing are introduced as people who establish prayer and spend from God's provision, a repeated foundational formulation of the two movements the section refuses to separate.

luna: The source's root ص ل و includes bounded ritual worship; this command pairs establishing ṣalāh with zakāh and communal bowing, placing formal prayer beside material duty. | terra: The command to establish prayer and give zakat is completed by bowing with those who bow, joining the source section's ritual boundary of ruku to its outgoing material obligation.

terra: Believers are told to seek help through patience and prayer; this gives prescribed prayer an inward sustaining effect, though it concerns the worshipper rather than a recipient's prayer for a giver.

luna: The section's poor, prayer, and charity belong together; this covenant names parents, kin, orphans, the miskīn, prayer, and zakāh, then says most turned away, a direct breach of that relation. | terra: The covenant joins care for parents, kin, orphans and the needy, good speech, prayer, and zakat; the ensuing turning-away is the same severance the section finds in surah 107.

luna: The section links ṣalāh to good that reaches beyond the worshipper; this command pairs prayer and zakāh with any good sent ahead to be found with God. | terra: The command joins prayer and zakat and says that whatever good people send ahead for themselves will be found with God, linking the material share to its inward and final return.
terra: The address to believers again makes patience and prayer means of seeking help, supporting the section's claim that salat should yield lived steadiness.

luna: The source distinguishes God's ṣalāh as purification or blessing; here God's ṣalawāt and mercy come upon the patient, giving a divine response that comforts those enduring hardship. | terra: The steadfast receive صلوات from their Lord together with mercy and guidance, another direct instance of divine salat as blessing rather than prescribed human ritual.

luna: The section makes prayer answer outwardly in aid: this account of al-birr joins giving wealth to kin, orphans, and the miskīn with prayer and zakāh, making those acts one lived righteousness. | terra: Righteousness is not exhausted by turning one's face in a ritual direction: it includes giving loved wealth to kin, orphans and the needy, establishing prayer, and giving zakat.

luna: The section's giving cycle needs a recipient; asked what to spend, this verse names parents, kin, orphans, the miskīn, and travelers as those who should receive good expenditure. | terra: When believers ask what to spend, the answer directs good wealth to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers, specifying the human destinations of the section's share.
terra: The command to guard the prayers and stand devoutly before God supplies the attentive constancy absent from the section's heedless worshippers.
terra: The ark's sign includes a سكينة from the Lord, showing repose as a divine gift borne by a concrete sign rather than by human prayer.

luna: The section's charity should purify and calm its recipient; this passage says spending loses its merit when followed by reminders or injury, guarding the receiver from the donor's self-display. | terra: Those who spend and do not follow their gift with reminders or hurt receive an end to fear and grief, showing how a gift can reach another without destroying the giver's promised repose.

luna: The section understands prayer as a comforting word directed to people; here a good word and pardon are better than charity followed by hurt, making the manner of giving part of its benefit. | terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt; material giving without the speech that preserves another's peace fails the section's outward-facing purpose.

luna: The section condemns a prayer aimed at being seen while withholding help; this warning explicitly pairs charity ruined by injury with spending for “riyāʾ al-nās,” exposing the same audience-facing piety. | terra: Charity is nullified by injury and by spending to be seen by people, extending the section's critique of spectator-facing worship directly into the use of wealth.

luna: The section says charity purifies the giver; this verse pictures spending to seek God's approval as a fruitful garden, directly contrasting the preceding warning against showy, harmful charity. | terra: Spending for God's pleasure and from firm inner conviction is pictured as a fruitful garden, giving an inward ground for the outward expenditure rather than a spectator's gaze.
terra: Believers must spend from the good things they have earned and not select inferior goods they themselves would accept only reluctantly, making the recipient's dignity part of genuine giving.
terra: Satan threatens poverty and commands indecency at the point of giving; this identifies the fear-driven pressure that can interrupt the section's movement of provision toward another.

luna: The section condemns prayer staged for sight; here giving charity openly is good but concealing it and giving it to the poor is better, and it erases sins, directing wealth away from display. | terra: Giving alms privately to the poor is better and expiates misdeeds, linking an actually delivered share, freedom from display, and purification.

luna: The section contrasts looking for an audience with care for another; this verse says expenditure for the poor is for the giver's own good and describes giving while seeking God's face. | terra: Whatever good believers spend is for their own souls, and they are to spend seeking God's face, linking outward benefit to inward return without public performance.

luna: The section asks that the miskīn receive what prayer should move a person to give; this verse depicts poor people devoted to God's way who need support but are mistaken for self-sufficient because of their restraint. | terra: Alms are for constrained poor people whom the uninformed may mistake for self-sufficient because they do not beg insistently, warning that public appearance can hide the person to whom the share is due.

luna: The section connects a material gift to reassurance; this verse describes people spending by night and day, secretly and openly, and promises them no fear or grief. | terra: Those who spend night and day, secretly and openly, are promised no fear or grief; both visible and hidden giving remain sound when their end is not the spectator.

luna: The section's prayer and gift are presented as one faithful practice; this verse pairs prayer and zakāh with a promise that the faithful need not fear or grieve. | terra: Belief and good works are specified through prayer and zakat, and culminate in freedom from fear and grief, joining the section's prayer, wealth, and repose.

luna: The section's charity purifies its giver; this verse says one will not attain al-birr until spending from what one loves, tying costly generosity to moral worth. | terra: People do not attain righteousness until they spend from what they love, making the movement of valued property outward a test of inward truth.
terra: An upright group recites God's signs at night while prostrating; 3:114 continues their embodied worship into enjoining right and hastening in good deeds.
terra: The night worshippers of 3:113 believe, enjoin right, forbid wrong, and hasten to good, showing prostration expressed through conduct toward the community.

luna: The section makes giving part of worship's effect on relationships; this portrait of the God-conscious joins spending in ease and hardship with restraining anger and pardoning people. | terra: The God-fearing spend in ease and hardship, restrain anger, and pardon people, placing material generosity beside inward restraint and restored relations.

terra: After the believers' failure, the Messenger is told to pardon them and seek forgiveness for them; this outward prayer belongs to a sequence of gentleness that keeps the community from dispersing.

luna: The section treats prayer as inseparable from duties to people; this command to worship God is followed by kindness to relatives, orphans, the miskīn, and neighbors. | terra: Worship of God is immediately expressed through goodness to parents, kin, orphans, the needy, neighbors, and travelers, while proud boasting is rejected.

luna: The section's worshippers keep property from others; this verse describes misers who urge miserliness and conceal God's bounty, a direct reversal of the outward gift that should accompany prayer. | terra: The condemned people are stingy, command others to stinginess, and conceal God's bounty; 4:38 then shows the apparently opposite act of spending corrupted by display.

luna: The section's spectacle-facing prayer leaves the needy without its benefit; this verse describes those who spend to be seen by people, linking ostentation directly to the use of wealth. | terra: Some spend their wealth only to be seen by people; beside the withholding of 4:37, this gives the same two public failures as the section: refusal and performance.
terra: Those intoxicated are forbidden to approach prayer until they know what they are saying, drawing a boundary around conscious presence that exposes heedless ritual.
terra: Those who wrong themselves are to come to the Messenger and have him seek forgiveness for them; his prayer on their behalf participates in their return to divine mercy.

luna: The section's prayer has a face directed toward other people; this verse identifies charitable giving, good conduct, or reconciliation as the few kinds of private counsel that are good when done seeking God's approval.
terra: The hypocrites rise lazily for prayer, showing themselves to people and remembering God only a little; this precisely exposes the spectator-facing prayer whose heart has gone elsewhere.

terra: Israel's covenant joins prayer and zakat to supporting the messengers and lending God a good loan, with expiation and gardens promised, so ritual, wealth, and cleansing consequence remain connected.
terra: Believers are described as establishing prayer and giving zakat while bowing, bringing ritual posture and the transferred share into a single portrait.
terra: God makes the night a سكن, using the same root for temporal and bodily rest that the section uses for the inward repose conveyed by prayer.
terra: The harvest's due must be given on harvest day, a particularly concrete instance of separating a share when provision becomes available.
terra: Humanity's mate is made so that one may يَسْكُنَ إِلَيْهَا, another direct use of settling toward a beloved person that clarifies prayer as relational refuge.
terra: True believers' hearts tremble at God's mention and grow in faith when His signs are recited; 8:3 gives that inward state the acts of prayer and spending.

luna: The section makes worship issue in generosity; this description of believers pairs establishing prayer with spending from what God has provided them. | terra: Those inwardly affected believers establish prayer and spend from what God provided, keeping both faces of worship in one description.
terra: The opponents' prayer at the House is reduced to whistling and clapping, another form in which visible ritual action has lost its proper substance and effect.
luna: The section says prayer and giving cannot be separated; in this post-conflict boundary, repentance, establishing prayer, and giving zakāh precede release from hostilities.

luna: The section says ṣalāh and charity are bound to social obligation; this verse makes repentance, maintaining prayer, and giving zakāh the condition for becoming brothers in religion. | terra: Repentance, established prayer, and zakat make former opponents brothers in religion, showing that the paired practices have a concrete communal relation.

luna: The section's ṣalāh is tested by its relation to the community; this verse describes God's mosques as maintained by those who believe, establish prayer, and give zakāh. | terra: Those who maintain God's mosques establish prayer, give zakat, and fear none but God, giving a visible place of worship an inward orientation and an outward material duty.

luna: The source's root س ك ن links the needy person with repose; after battle panic, this verse says God sent sakīnah upon His Messenger and the believers, a parallel picture of reassurance arriving to people. | terra: God sends His سكينة upon the Messenger and believers amid battle, a communal form of divinely bestowed repose under fear.

luna: The section says property should move to the needy rather than be withheld; this warning targets those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way. | terra: Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way embody the retained wealth at the opposite pole from the section's purifying charity cycle.

luna: The section treats sakan as calm given to another; this verse says God sent sakīnah upon His Messenger in the cave, a divine reassurance rather than a human prayer. | terra: In the cave God sends His سكينة upon the Messenger after the assurance not to grieve, making repose the answer to acute fear.

luna: The section says the prayer's social face is severed when the share is withheld; this description of hypocrites pairs their reluctant prayer with reluctant spending and shows the same split as deliberate hypocrisy. | terra: Lazy attendance at prayer and unwilling spending occur together as reasons the hypocrites' expenditures are not accepted, matching both broken links in the section.

luna: The section says the Prophet's prayer should bring its recipients tranquility; this account of charity recipients says they rejoice if given a share but become angry if not, showing the self-interested response the cycle must overcome.

luna: The section's prayer-and-giving cycle ends at the poor; this verse names the miskīn among the recipients of obligatory charities, making the transfer's destination concrete. | terra: The prescribed recipients of alms include the poor and needy, making concrete where the share identified with maun as zakat must go.

luna: The section's hypocrites close their social hand while retaining religious appearance; this description of hypocrite men and women says they close their hands and forget God, a direct likeness of withholding help. | terra: Hypocrites enjoin wrong, forbid right, and close their hands; forgetting God and withholding from others are presented as the same inward disorder.

luna: The section says worship has a face turned toward other people; here believing men and women are each other's allies, maintain prayer, give zakāh, and seek God's mercy, placing the paired acts in mutual care. | terra: Believing men and women are allies who enjoin right, forbid wrong, establish prayer, and give zakat, the communal positive opposite of 9:67 and the section's isolated performance.
terra: Some covenant that if God gives them bounty they will give charity; 9:76-77 reveals the broken promise as withholding that produces hypocrisy within.

luna: The section describes people withholding what should reach others; here, after receiving God's bounty, people are said to have withheld it and turned away, a specific reversal of the charitable cycle. | terra: When bounty comes, they become stingy with it and turn away, enacting the moment at which wealth ceases to move outward.

luna: The section describes prayer emptied of sincerity; this neighbor to 9:76 says their broken pledge and lies left hypocrisy in their hearts, naming the inward consequence of withholding after a promise. | terra: Their broken promise and lying leave hypocrisy in their hearts, showing the inward result of the withheld bounty in 9:75-76.

luna: The section exposes piety performed for an audience; here hypocrites mock believers who contribute generously or can offer only little, showing how public judgment can attack the very giving the section calls for.
terra: The Messenger's seeking forgiveness cannot benefit these hypocrites even if repeated; 9:84 then expresses that boundary with the verb of salat itself.

terra: The Messenger is forbidden to perform salat over a dead hypocrite, a sharp boundary showing that outward-directed salat can be withheld by divine judgment rather than emptied by human indifference.

luna: The section presents expenditure as a path to nearness and tranquility; these Bedouins regard what they spend as a fine and expect harm to befall the believers, a specific contrary stance toward giving.

luna: The section links property given to a prayer that settles its recipients; here the Bedouins' expenditures are “qurubāt” and the Messenger's prayers are named as a further nearness to God. | terra: Some Bedouin believers treat what they spend as nearness to God and as a means to the Messenger's صلوات; it confirms that giving can elicit the outward-directed prayer described in the section.

luna: This is the section's stated cycle: charity from property purifies the giver, then the Prophet's prayer (salli ʿalayhim) is “sakanun lahum”; it joins giving, tazkiyah, and reassurance in one act. | terra: This is the section's complete cycle: a share is taken from wealth to cleanse and purify its givers, the Messenger prays over them, and his صلات is a سكن for them.

luna: The section presents charity as a purifying gift received by God; this neighbor to 9:103 says God accepts repentance and takes the charities, completing the divine side of the transfer. | terra: Immediately after the section's central verse, God is named as the one who accepts repentance and takes charities, completing the movement of the offered share beyond the human exchange in 9:103.
terra: The Prophet and believers are forbidden to seek forgiveness for known idolaters after their fate is clear, defining a boundary around prayer offered on another person's behalf.
terra: The night is made so people may rest in it, an environmental form of سكن that parallels the prayer functioning as repose for its recipients.

luna: The source's root ص ل و includes bounded ritual prayer, and the section argues that it reaches the use of wealth; Shuʿayb's opponents ask whether his prayer commands them to change how they deal with their property. | terra: Shuayb's opponents ask whether his صلاة commands them to change what they do with their wealth, explicitly recognizing the reach from worship into property.

terra: The command to establish prayer at the day's edges is followed by the statement that good deeds remove bad deeds, giving prescribed prayer a purifying moral effect rather than a merely visible form.
terra: Joseph's brothers ask their father to seek forgiveness for their sins, a direct request for one human being's prayer on behalf of others.
terra: Jacob promises to seek his Lord's forgiveness for them, completing the interhuman request of 12:97 with a prayer directed toward their restoration.
luna: The section links prayer with property reaching others; this account pairs establishing prayer with spending secretly and openly from provision, and says they answer evil with good.

luna: The section says the Prophet's prayer gives people repose; this verse describes hearts finding rest in remembering God, a nonlexical counterpart for how reassurance settles the inward person. | terra: Hearts find rest in God's remembrance; this supplies a nonlexical parallel for the inward repose that prayer is meant to carry, though here the verse speaks of remembrance rather than another person's supplication.

luna: The section's charity is a share sent beyond the self; this command pairs prayer with spending, secretly and openly, before a day without trade or friendship. | terra: Believing servants are told in one breath to establish prayer and spend secretly and openly before the day when ordinary exchanges fail.

luna: The section develops the source's root س ك ن as relational settling and repose; Ibrahim says he settled descendants near the sacred house so they may pray, then asks that hearts incline toward them and provision reach them.

luna: The source distinguishes ritual ṣalāh from supplication; Ibrahim asks to be made an establisher of prayer and then asks God to accept his duʿāʾ, putting both directions in one plea. | terra: Abraham asks to be made an establisher of ritual prayer and immediately asks God to accept his دعاء; the two senses developed by the section meet in one utterance.
terra: Abraham's next petition extends beyond himself to his parents and all believers, supplying the other-directed face of the prayer requested in 14:40.
terra: God makes houses a سكن, a material place of repose; this concrete sense clarifies what the section transfers to the Messenger's prayer as relational shelter.

luna: The section says the prayer's outward reach should meet need; this command assigns kin, the miskīn, and the traveler their due, naming concrete recipients of the wealth that the section's worshippers withhold. | terra: Kin, the needy, and the traveler are to be given their due, expressing the allocated obligation the section hears in maun as zakat.
terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended without limit, giving a concrete boundary between withholding the share and spending without measure.

luna: The source distinguishes ritual ṣalāh from its outward benefit; Jesus says he was enjoined with ṣalāh and zakāh for as long as he lives, joining worship to material duty. | terra: Jesus says that God charged him with prayer and zakat for as long as he lives, binding the two as one lifelong vocation rather than a display.

luna: The section argues that ṣalāh reaches beyond private performance; Ishmael is praised for ordering his family to prayer and zakāh, carrying worship into household conduct. | terra: Ishmael commands his household to prayer and zakat and is pleasing to his Lord, extending their union from the individual into family life.

luna: The section distinguishes real prayer from a hollow outward act; this verse says later people lost ṣalāh and followed desires, giving the inward failure its consequence. | terra: A later generation loses prayer and follows desires; this names the contrary condition in which salat no longer orders the inner life.
terra: God commands Moses to establish prayer for His remembrance, setting prayer's intended attentiveness against the heedlessness described in the section.
terra: The Messenger is told to command his family to prayer and persevere in it while God assumes responsibility for provision, placing sustained worship beside economic dependence on God.

luna: The section joins worship to active care; the guided leaders are described as doing good, establishing prayer, and giving zakāh, so the pair belongs to lived guidance. | terra: The appointed leaders are inspired to do good, establish prayer, and give zakat; worship and beneficent action belong to one divinely guided leadership.

luna: The section links an inward state of worship to spending for others; this portrait joins trembling hearts, patience, prayer, and spending from God's provision in the same description of the faithful. | terra: Humble hearts that tremble at God's mention are described together with steadfastness, established prayer, and spending from God's provision, joining heart, ritual, and gift.

luna: The section says worship must shape treatment of others; those established in the land are described as maintaining prayer and zakāh while enjoining right and forbidding wrong. | terra: Those given authority establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin right, and forbid wrong, showing public prayer completed by public moral and material responsibility.
terra: Believers are told to bow, prostrate, worship their Lord, and do good so that they may prosper; 22:78 continues this embodied worship with prayer and zakat.
terra: After the bowing, prostration, and good action of 22:77, this ayah commands prayer and zakat together and tells believers to hold fast to God.

luna: The source's root ص ل و includes formal prayer, whose inner orientation the section says is missing; these successful believers are humble in their prayers, the opposite of heedlessness. | terra: Successful believers are humble within their prayer, the inward posture missing from a merely visible ritual.

luna: The section joins prayer's inward purpose to giving; this portrait places zakāh among the deeds of successful believers, between turning from idle speech and guarding chastity. | terra: The same believers are active in zakat, so the humble prayer of 23:2 does not stop at the self but has an outgoing material counterpart.

luna: The section condemns being heedless about ṣalāh; this portrait closes by saying successful believers guard their prayers, a direct reversal of that neglect. | terra: Believers carefully guard their prayers, the positive boundary opposite neglecting or being absent from them.

terra: People of bounty are forbidden to cease giving to kin, the needy, and emigrants and are told to pardon and overlook if they desire God's forgiveness, binding continued provision to relational healing.

luna: The section connects worship to how wealth is handled; this verse says trade and sale do not distract believers from remembrance, prayer, and zakāh, directly setting commerce beside worship. | terra: Neither trade nor sale distracts these people from remembrance, prayer, or zakat; economic life remains joined to attentive worship and giving.

luna: The section's cycle joins prayer and giving to reassurance; this verse commands prayer, zakāh, and obedience to the Messenger, then points to receiving mercy. | terra: Prayer and zakat are commanded together with obedience to the Messenger so that mercy may be received, joining the ritual and material acts to a relational outcome.

terra: Believers who seek the Messenger's permission in a communal matter are granted it and receive his prayer for forgiveness, another concrete setting for prophetic supplication on behalf of believers.
terra: The servants of the Merciful spend the night prostrating and standing before their Lord; 25:67 later gives this same portrait a disciplined way of spending wealth.
terra: Their spending is neither wasteful nor stingy but held to a just measure, so the night worship of 25:64 reaches the use of property without collapsing into refusal.
terra: The night is made for people to rest and the day to see, repeating the created rhythm of repose behind the section's relational use of the same root.
terra: The challenge asks who besides God could bring a night in which people rest if daylight were perpetual, marking repose as a provision that cannot be produced at will.

luna: The section asks what prayer does within a person; this verse says ṣalāh restrains indecency and wrong, stating the moral work that the hollow worshippers have lost. | terra: Prayer is said to restrain indecency and wrongdoing; it therefore should work within the person rather than remain the intact-looking shell described in the section.

luna: The source's dictionary gloss for س ك ن is whatever beloved thing one finds rest in; this verse says spouses are created so each may find tranquility with the other, extending that relational comfort beyond the charity scene. | terra: Spouses are created so that one may لِتَسْكُنُوا إِلَيْهَا, with affection and mercy between them; this is the relational repose captured by the section's dictionary definition of sakan.

luna: The section connects property, the miskīn, and seeking divine acceptance; this verse assigns the poor and traveler their due and says this is best for those seeking God's face. | terra: The command again directs each due to kin, the needy, and the traveler, and calls that course good for those seeking God's face.
terra: Those who leave their beds call upon their Lord in fear and hope and spend from His provision, joining supplication, inward stance, and outward giving in one ayah.

terra: The Prophet's household is told to avoid public display, establish prayer, and give zakat, and the same ayah speaks of God's will to remove impurity and purify them; it gathers display, ritual, gift, and purification in one setting.

luna: The source's root ص ل و includes God's ṣalāh as an act of cleansing; this verse says God and the angels send ṣalāh on believers to bring them from darkness into light. | terra: God and His angels perform صلاة upon the believers in order to bring them from darkness into light, directly illustrating the source section's dictionary sense of God's salat as purifying beneficence.

luna: The source distinguishes human prayer from God's action of ṣalāh; this verse commands believers themselves to send ṣalāh on the Prophet, showing the word's interpersonal use beyond ritual prayer. | terra: God and the angels perform salat upon the Prophet, and believers are told to do so too; salat here is explicitly directed toward another rather than enclosed within the worshipper.

luna: The section joins prayer to the use of property; this verse pairs prayer with secret and public expenditure and calls it a trade that will not perish. | terra: Those who recite God's book, establish prayer, and spend secretly and openly hope for a trade that will not perish, redirecting economic imagery into worship and gift.

terra: When commanded to spend from God's provision, disbelievers refuse by asking why they should feed someone God could feed, exposing a theological excuse for stopping provision before it reaches the hungry.
terra: The night worshipper alternates prostration and standing while fearing the Hereafter and hoping for divine mercy, giving the visible postures a stated inward consciousness.
terra: God makes the night for rest and the day for sight, again presenting سكن as a bestowed good before the section applies it to another person's prayer.

luna: The section treats worship as a communal practice with material consequences; this portrait of believers pairs prayer and spending from their provision with consultation over their affairs. | terra: Those who respond to their Lord establish prayer, conduct affairs by mutual counsel, and spend from His provision, making prayer part of reciprocal communal life.
terra: People called to spend include some who withhold, and the verse says that such withholding is against oneself, exposing the inward damage caused by breaking the outward movement.

luna: The source's root س ك ن links the miskīn with repose; this verse says God sends sakīnah into believers' hearts, a parallel account of calm settling within a community. | terra: God sends السكينة into believers' hearts so their faith may increase, locating repose within the heart just as the section says prayer settles the giver inwardly.

luna: The section's “sakanun lahum” makes tranquility a gift to people; this verse says God sent sakīnah upon the believers at the pledge, echoing reassurance in a communal bond. | terra: God knows what is in the believers' hearts and sends سكينة upon them, explicitly connecting the bestowed calm with inward knowledge.
terra: Against the opponents' heated pride, God sends سكينة upon His Messenger and believers, defining tranquility by its opposite social posture.

terra: The Messenger's companions are seen bowing and prostrating while seeking God's bounty and pleasure; the visible trace of prostration is grounded in an explicitly God-directed intention rather than spectatorship.
terra: The God-fearing sleep little at night; 51:18-19 continues their hidden devotion through seeking forgiveness and recognizing another person's right in their wealth.
terra: Their pre-dawn seeking of forgiveness supplies the supplicatory act between the night devotion of 51:17 and the allocated wealth-share of 51:19.

luna: The section says the needy should receive what the worshipper withholds; this account of the God-fearing says their property contains a due for the asker and the deprived. | terra: The God-fearing have a right in their wealth for the asker and deprived, an exact positive counterpart to refusing to set aside the section's share.
luna: The section links giving wealth with purification; this verse describes charitable men and women and those who lend God a good loan, making material generosity an act of worship.

terra: After believers shrink from advancing charity before private consultation with the Messenger, they are directed to prayer, zakat, and obedience, keeping interpersonal access and wealth accountable to worship.

luna: The section sends a share of property toward people in need; this rule for distributing communal wealth names the poor and other recipients and says it should not circulate only among the rich. | terra: The distribution to kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers is ordered so wealth will not circulate only among the rich, stating the social purpose of an outward-moving share.
terra: Poor emigrants seeking God's bounty and pleasure are identified before the Helpers prefer them in 59:9, distinguishing the receiving people whose need activates that generosity.

luna: The section's giver sets aside a share instead of hoarding it; these believers prefer others over themselves even in need, and the verse calls success freedom from the soul's stinginess. | terra: The Helpers prefer others even amid their own need, and success belongs to those guarded from inner stinginess; outward provision and inward cleansing coincide.
terra: Later believers pray for earlier believers and ask that rancor be removed from their own hearts, joining an outward-directed supplication to inward cleansing and relational peace.
terra: After believing women make their pledge, the Messenger is told to seek God's forgiveness for them, another communal setting in which prophetic prayer accompanies a material and moral covenant.
terra: At the call to Friday prayer believers must leave trade and hasten to remembrance, establishing a boundary in which commerce yields to attentive worship.
terra: After prayer they may disperse, seek God's bounty, and remember Him much, reintegrating prayer with economic life rather than leaving the two unrelated.
terra: When invited to let the Messenger seek forgiveness for them, the hypocrites turn their heads away in arrogance, refusing the very other-directed prophetic prayer that could accompany return.
terra: The hypocrites explicitly urge others not to spend on those around the Messenger until they disperse, turning withheld provision into a means of breaking community.
luna: The section condemns withholding the share due to others; facing death, a person regrets delay and asks to give charity and become righteous, showing the lost opportunity to give.
terra: Hearing and obeying are joined to spending, and success is tied to protection from the soul's stinginess, making the gift an inward transformation as well as an outward act.
terra: The spending commanded in 64:16 becomes a good loan that God multiplies and forgives, completing the movement from resistance to stinginess toward acceptance and pardon.

luna: The section says the prayerful should not withhold what reaches the needy; these garden owners agree to keep a poor person from entering their harvest, staging that refusal as a deliberate act. | terra: The garden owners whisper that no needy person is to enter upon them that day, staging the deliberate exclusion of the poor from provision.
terra: They go out believing themselves able to prevent access to the crop, continuing 68:24's scene of withholding the poor person's share.
terra: The condemned person's refusal to believe in God is immediately followed in 69:34 by failure to urge feeding the needy, mirroring denial and social refusal as one moral break.

luna: The section's cycle turns worship toward the miskīn, while this account of the denier says he did not urge feeding the poor; it states the same failed social duty as a cause of ruin. | terra: He did not urge the feeding of the needy, the same concrete omission named in 107:3 and tied here by 69:33 to disbelief.
terra: The sequence declares the human being created anxious and grasping; 70:20-25 unfolds this condition and then excepts worshippers whose wealth contains a known right.
terra: When harm touches the anxious person he becomes panicked; the ensuing verses contrast this unsettled inward state with constant prayer and provision for others.

luna: The section's hypocrites retain a religious appearance but withhold aid; this portrait says people hold back when good reaches them, then immediately sets the praying people apart. | terra: Human beings become withholding when good reaches them; 70:22-25 immediately except enduring worshippers who reserve a known share in their wealth for others.

luna: The section says prayer's inward and outward sides have been split; this verse makes the praying people an exception to withholding (70:21), and 70:23–25 specify their constancy and the due in their property. | terra: The phrase "except those who pray" begins the exception to the anxious, withholding person of 70:19-21, and 70:23-25 explains that exception through constant prayer and a wealth-share for others.

luna: The section condemns people heedless about their ṣalāh; this passage describes people constant in ṣalāh, and 70:24–25 immediately show that their constancy includes a known due for the asker and deprived. | terra: These worshippers remain constant in their prayer, the positive reversal of a heart absent from prayer; 70:24-25 then gives that constancy an outward economic face.

luna: The section's cycle moves from worship to a portion of wealth for someone else; this passage gives the constant worshippers a “known due” in their property, and 70:25 identifies its recipients as asker and deprived. | terra: Their wealth contains a حق معلوم, a known right, making explicit the apportioned share that the section says is withheld.

luna: The section connects prayer with the miskīn's unmet need; this verse names the asker and deprived as recipients of a known claim on the worshippers' property, specified in 70:24. | terra: The known right of 70:24 is directed to the asker and the deprived, so the prayerful person's allotted wealth actually reaches another person.
terra: Guarding prayer closes the ethical portrait begun at 70:22-25, showing that the wealth-share belongs inside a sustained life of prayer.

luna: The source's root ص ل و denotes ritual prayer in one branch, while the section joins it to the zakāh represented by Maʿūn; this verse pairs prayer and zakāh with a good loan to God. | terra: The command to establish prayer and give zakat is followed by lending God a good loan, making the material outward movement part of what is found with God.

luna: The section's men keep the name of prayer while failing the needy; in the answer about Saqar, the condemned say they were not among those who prayed, and 74:44 adds that they did not feed the miskīn, setting true prayer beside care for the poor. | terra: The people of Saqar confess that they were not among those who prayed; 74:44 and 74:46 complete the same triad of failed prayer, failed feeding, and denial found in surah 107.

luna: The section treats the hungry person's unmet need as the break in prayer's outward reach; this answer names “feeding the miskīn” as a reason for ruin, while 74:43 supplies the companion failure to pray. | terra: Their next confession is that they did not feed the needy, placing neglected care directly beside the neglected prayer of 74:43.
terra: Their denial of the Day of Judgment completes the sequence begun by non-prayer and non-feeding in 74:43-44, reproducing the moral structure of the whole surah behind this image.
terra: The condemned person neither affirms nor prays; 75:32 adds that he denies and turns away, reversing surah 107's combination of denial with an outward prayer-shell.
terra: Denial and turning away explain the non-prayer of 75:31; surah 107 internalizes that same turning-away inside people still called worshippers.

luna: The section traces property given toward a needy person; here the righteous give food to the miskīn, orphan, and captive despite loving it, embodying the outward generosity its hypocrites withhold. | terra: The righteous give food, despite loving it, to the needy, orphan, and captive, supplying the outward act absent from the section's worshippers.

luna: The section contrasts worship turned toward spectators with a prayer meant to benefit another; these feeders say they seek God's face and want neither repayment nor thanks, clarifying the motive behind 76:8's gift. | terra: They feed solely for God's face and want neither recompense nor thanks, the clearest positive reversal of an act turned toward spectators.
terra: Success belongs to the person who purifies himself; 87:15 immediately joins that purification to remembering the Lord and praying.
terra: Remembering the Lord's name and praying follows self-purification in 87:14, bringing salat and tazkiya into the same short sequence.
terra: Failure to honor the orphan begins a sequence that continues with not urging food for the needy and consuming wealth, recalling the vulnerable people displaced by empty worship.

luna: The section's 107:3 background is the failure to urge food for the poor; this rebuke says they do not urge one another to feed the miskīn, making the lost social obligation explicit. | terra: The people do not urge one another to feed the needy; 89:19-20 locates that neglect beside voracious consumption and love of wealth.
terra: After failure to honor the orphan and urge feeding the needy, the people consume inheritance voraciously, identifying misdirected acquisition behind the social refusal.

luna: The section condemns worshippers who withhold what should reach the poor; this verse says people love wealth intensely, supplying the inward attachment behind refusal to urge food for the miskīn in 89:18. | terra: Their excessive love of wealth closes the sequence begun by neglecting the orphan and needy, naming the attachment that prevents the share from moving outward.

luna: The section's hungry person is left without the aid that should issue from worship; this verse names feeding on a day of hunger as the needed act. | terra: The steep path includes feeding on a day of hunger; 90:15-16 identifies the orphan and destitute person to whom that provision moves.
terra: The first recipient in the feeding scene is a related orphan, keeping material care embedded in a human bond.

luna: The section connects the miskīn to nourishment and a share of wealth; this verse identifies a “miskīnan dhā matrabah,” a poor person in the dust. | terra: The second recipient is a needy person in misery, completing the concrete opposite of a share that never reaches anyone.

luna: The section's positive cycle begins with giving and ends in purification and reassurance; this verse's contrasting portrait is of one who gives and is mindful of God, the charitable path set against the miser in 92:8.

luna: The section's action releases wealth to bring purification and peace; this opposing portrait joins miserliness with thinking oneself self-sufficient, the stance that closes off the transfer. | terra: The contrary figure is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient; 92:9-11 develops his denial, hard path, and wealth's failure to save him.
terra: His stinginess is joined to denial of the best promise, reproducing the link between refusal and denial that stands behind surah 107.
terra: The miser who denies is eased toward hardship, reversing the ease and satisfaction promised to the purifying giver later in the same surah.
terra: His wealth will not avail him when he falls, exposing the ultimate failure of property kept inward rather than given for purification.

luna: The section's Tevbe 9:103 says charity purifies its giver; this person “yuʾtī mālahu yatazakkā,” giving wealth in order to purify himself, a direct parallel to that cycle. | terra: The God-fearing person gives his wealth in order to purify himself, a compact parallel to the charity that purifies its giver in 9:103.
terra: The giver of 92:18 is not merely repaying someone's favor, clarifying that his purifying gift is not a social performance or exchange.

luna: The section warns that prayer performed for spectators has lost its outward purpose; this verse says he seeks only his Lord's face, supplying the opposite audience for giving. | terra: He gives seeking only the face of his Most High Lord, the positive reversal of orienting an act toward human spectators.
terra: The giver will be satisfied, furnishing an affective end to the sequence of wealth, purification, and sincere direction in 92:18-20.
terra: The command not to oppress the orphan is the direct positive boundary against the repulsion of the orphan in surah 107's larger scene.
terra: The command not to rebuff the asker supplies the outward responsiveness absent when maun is withheld.

luna: The section contrasts prayer meant for spectators with prayer's true purpose; this verse frames worship as sincere devotion and pairs establishing prayer with giving zakāh. | terra: Sincere worship is defined together with establishing prayer and giving zakat, making sincerity the bond between ritual and the outgoing share.
terra: God feeds Quraysh against hunger and gives security against fear; the pairing of provision and safety is the divine counterpart to the section's human movement from a share to repose.
